tldr: By using a large-scale pretrained motion generation model as a frozen backbone directly for action generation and combining it with a lightweight visual adapter and a hierarchical structure, this work achieves humanoid control with high-dimensional whole-body coordination.
hero_caption: Overview of the Kimodo-Policy architecture and achievements. It adopts a three-stage Root-Body-Hand architecture that keeps a pretrained motion generation model (Kimodo) frozen and injects visual information via a lightweight ControlNet. It outperforms strong baselines in both simulation and real-world tasks.
overview:
In humanoid "loco-manipulation," such as picking up an object while walking, it is necessary to temporally and spatially coordinate high-dimensional whole-body joint movements—not just end-effector manipulation, but also trunk balance and foot stepping. While popular Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World Action Models (WAMs) acquire semantic language understanding or physical video dynamics through pretraining, they do not necessarily capture the kinematic coordination structure specific to humanoids directly.

To address this, the authors propose a new paradigm called Kinematic Action Models (KAMs): pretraining directly on motion itself and reusing the motion generator as the foundation for an action model. Its concrete implementation is "Kimodo-Policy." It uses "Kimodo," a pretrained text-to-motion model, as a frozen backbone and injects first-person camera images using a lightweight ControlNet. The overall architecture is organized into a three-stage hierarchy—root trajectory → body joints → bimanual hand manipulation. By repeatedly conditioning on past motion history and predicting short action chunks, it turns open-loop motion generation into real-time closed-loop control.

Evaluation was conducted across humanoid benchmarks, including HumanoidArena (7 tasks) and SIMPLE (8 tasks), as well as 8 whole-body coordination tasks on a real Unitree G1 robot. Kimodo-Policy achieved a peak success rate of 72.14% in HumanoidArena multi-task learning and an average success rate of 60% on the real robot, outperforming existing VLA- and WAM-based methods. Ablation experiments also demonstrate that keeping the pretrained motion backbone frozen yields substantially higher performance than randomly initializing or fine-tuning it.
contributions: Proposed Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a new paradigm that directly reuses motion generation models as the foundational backbone for action generation.
Constructed Kimodo-Policy, a lightweight three-stage architecture that injects vision into a frozen motion model via ControlNet and sequentially predicts root, body, and hands.
Connected the motion generation model to closed-loop whole-body tracking control through constraints from past motion history and repeated prediction of action chunks.
Experimentally proved the effectiveness of motion pretraining by achieving a top success rate of 72.14% on HumanoidArena and an average success rate of 60% across 8 real-world tasks.

sections.heading: Why pretrain directly on motion instead of just vision and language?
sections.summary: High-dimensional whole-body coordination is indispensable for loco-manipulation, but visual and semantic priors from existing VLAs and WAMs cannot fully represent the kinematic structure of a robot. The authors propose KAMs using motion generation models directly as action backbones, demonstrating the effectiveness of Kimodo-Policy in simulation and real-world experiments.
sections.details:
Humanoid loco-manipulation is not just an extension of arm manipulation. Reaching for an object while walking toward a target requires simultaneously coordinating the pelvis (root), trunk, arms, and legs while maintaining the body's center of mass. In other words, generating whole-body motion is not merely an "auxiliary execution component" of task planning; it lies at the very core of task completion.

Mainstream VLAs inherit semantic understanding from vision-language models, and WAMs inherit world dynamics from video generation models. However, they do not directly learn the kinematic structure—how the robot's multiple joints coordinate and move together. Trying to learn this complex whole-body coordination from scratch using only downstream reinforcement learning or imitation learning demands massive amounts of data and trial-and-error.

This led to the question: can motion generation itself serve as the pretraining target for foundation models? Kinematic Action Models (KAMs) proposed in this work position a motion generation model, pretrained on large-scale human motion capture data, directly as the main action backbone. This allows task learning to begin with prior knowledge of temporal and cross-body coordination patterns from the outset.

The first realization of this is Kimodo-Policy. It freezes the text-to-motion model "Kimodo" and injects visual features via a lightweight ControlNet. By dividing the body into three stages—root, body, and hands—and performing receding-horizon control that predicts and executes future motion chunks conditioned on past motion history, it adapts the generative model to real-time interaction. Out of a total of 678M parameters, only 92M are trainable.

captions.F2: Comparison of pretraining backbones for action generation. From left to right: VLA (Vision-Language Model), WAM (World Action Model), and KAM (Kinematic Action Model, proposed in this paper). KAM directly passes the kinematic structure embedded in the motion generator to downstream trackers, placing it at the core of the action model.

sections.heading: A new approach at the intersection of whole-body control, motion pretraining, and motion generation
sections.summary: Prior studies explored whole-body control via VLAs/WAMs or utilized human motion data in an auxiliary role. Unlike these approaches, KAMs directly reuse a pretrained motion generation model as the main backbone, feeding the robot's kinematic structure directly into action generation.
sections.details:
To understand where this work stands, let us look at three related research areas.

### Whole-Body Control and Loco-Manipulation
Research on humanoid whole-body control is progressing rapidly, including HumanVLA, which distills an RL-trained teacher model, OASIS, which leverages simulation teleoperation, and foundation model approaches like GR00T N1 and $\Psi_{0}$. World Action Models (WAMs) predicting future visual states have also emerged. However, while these strengthen perception or predictive dynamics, they are not based on models that directly generate intricate, coordinated whole-body kinematics.

### Motion Pretraining for Robot Control
There have also been attempts to incorporate human motion data. Approaches like Humanoid-VLA treat motion inside language models, while Being-M0.7 injects predictive features from vision and motion into separate action experts. Yet, most of these treat motion as semantic latent representations or align it with separate expert pathways. KAMs set themselves apart by using the motion generator itself as the primary backbone for final action generation, directly sending kinematic commands to the tracker.

### Advances in Motion Generation Models
Motion models have made substantial strides in animation and character control, with diffusion models for text-to-motion (MDM, MLD) and constrained generation (OmniControl). In particular, "Kimodo" enables large-scale motion capture training, a hierarchical diffusion process for root and body, and diverse keyframe controls. Kimodo-Policy bridges this mature motion generation capability to robotic manipulation through visual adaptation and closed-loop control.

sections.heading: Breathing vision into a frozen backbone for closed-loop control
sections.summary: Kimodo-Policy uses a three-stage structure: it injects visual information into the frozen Kimodo root and body denoisers via ControlNet and controls both hands with an independent HandNet. Smooth closed-loop control is achieved by constraining past motion history as an input prefix while predicting future action chunks.
sections.details:
Here is how the architecture and control loop adapt a motion generation model for closed-loop robotic control.

### 3.1 Foundations: Kimodo and ControlNet
The base model, "Kimodo-G1," is a hierarchical diffusion model that generates robot motion trajectories from language instructions. After predicting the root (global translation and heading), it generates joint motions conditioned on that root. Kimodo-Policy keeps these Kimodo weights completely frozen. Introducing the "ControlNet" method widely used in image generation, it injects egocentric camera features residually into Kimodo's internal layers via zero-initialized projection layers from trainable control branches.

### 3.2 Three-Stage Model Architecture
The overall architecture is divided into three stages: Root, Body, and Hand.
- **Language and Vision Encoders**: Text instructions are tokenized with LLM2Vec, and egocentric images are tokenized with a frozen DINOv3.
- **Dual-Path Fusion**: When incorporating visual features into the ControlNet branch, two paths are fused: cross-attention for "selective retrieval of necessary visual information" and an MLP for "direct mapping from image tokens to the future time horizon."
- **Stop-Gradient**: Stop-gradient ($\operatorname{sg}$) operations are placed at the interfaces from root to body and body to hands. This is designed so that hand learning losses do not disrupt body and root motion generation.
- **HandNet**: Because opening and closing hand grippers differs fundamentally from joint pose trajectories, an independent diffusion head, "HandNet," predicts left and right hand open/close states conditioned on body features and visual information.

### 3.3 Closed-Loop Adaptation of Motion Pretraining
The key to using a generative model for interactive control is "motion history conditioning." Within a temporal window centered at the current time step, past motion history (up to 100 frames) is masked and enforced as a fixed constraint, and the diffusion model is tasked with inpainting only the future chunk (50 frames, ~1.67 seconds). The robot executes only the first 15 frames (0.5 seconds) of this prediction and repeats this in a receding-horizon control loop with updated observations and history.

### 3.4 Training Objectives and Inference
The loss function is a weighted sum of Mean Squared Error (MSE) on the root and body, hand reconstruction loss, and a hand transition loss ($\ell_1$ norm) to suppress abrupt hand changes. During inference, DDIM is used for fast 10-step denoising, and predicted root and joint trajectories are sent to the low-level whole-body tracker "SONIC" to execute at 50Hz.

Bottom: Kimodo-Policy carrying a banana on the real robot by repeatedly predicting and executing chunks based on past motion history and new visual observations.

sections.heading: Large-scale pretraining and diverse evaluations across simulation and real robots
sections.summary: After pretraining the visual adaptation branch on 419 hours of humanoid manipulation demonstration data, the model was evaluated on HumanoidArena, SIMPLE, and a real Unitree G1 robot. On the real robot, demonstrations for 8 tasks were collected and validated using a PICO-based teleoperation system.
sections.details:
To evaluate the proposed method rigorously, the authors established a large dataset and testing environments.

### 4.1 Policy Pretraining
While keeping the motion backbone frozen, a 419-hour robot manipulation corpus was assembled from three public datasets (HIW-500, 14 subsets of UniFoLM-WBT, and Humanoid Everyday) to adapt the vision-injecting ControlNet and HandNet. Left and right hand states were unified into a 2D vector in $[-1, 1]$ to absorb variations across different robot hand morphologies. Pretraining was run on 16 NVIDIA H200 GPUs with a batch size of 1024 for about 60 hours (1 million steps).

### 4.2 Post-Training and Evaluation Benchmarks
Downstream evaluation was conducted on three platforms:
- **HumanoidArena**: A simulation benchmark consisting of 7 tasks where lower-body motion is critical (Soccer, MoveDesk, CarryBox, OpenDoor, SitSofa, Boxing, and VisualNav). Both single-task fine-tuning and multi-task learning across all 7 tasks with a single policy are evaluated. Success Rate (SR) and Average Fall Rate (AFR) are measured.
- **SIMPLE**: An environment combining MuJoCo contact physics with Isaac Sim rendering, evaluating 8 tasks including handovers, door opening/closing, and chair pushing/pulling. Robustness is tested across three difficulty levels (L0 to L2) with randomized appearances, lighting, and object placements.
- **Real-Robot Validation (Unitree G1)**: A whole-body teleoperation system was built with an operator wearing a PICO 4 Ultra headset, controllers, and trackers. 25–30 demonstration episodes were collected for each of 8 tasks (such as punch bag, sit on cushion, bimanual pick-and-place, and push cart) to measure real-world success rates.

sections.heading: Outperforming VLAs and WAMs: ablations highlight the power of freezing motion
sections.summary: Kimodo-Policy achieved a peak success rate of 72.14% in HumanoidArena multi-task learning and an average success rate of 60% on the real robot. Ablation studies clearly demonstrated the advantage of keeping the motion backbone frozen and the importance of motion pretraining quality.
sections.details:
Key findings from the experiments include:

### 5.1 & 5.2 Superior Coordination in Simulation
In the HumanoidArena multi-task evaluation, Kimodo-Policy* (with pretraining) achieved an overall success rate of 72.14%, outperforming strong baselines such as GR00T N1.7 (69.70%) and GigaWorld-Policy (68.39%). Its Average Fall Rate (AFR) was also the lowest at roughly 4.3%. It showed exceptional strength in Human-Scene Interaction (HSI) tasks, such as sitting on a sofa (SitSofa: 96.7%) and opening a door (OpenDoor: 93.3%). On the SIMPLE benchmark, it reached an average success rate of 75.83%, on par with or exceeding the leading baseline $\Psi_{0}$ (75.42%).

### 5.3 Real-World Robot Evaluation
Across 8 tasks on the real G1 robot, the version trained directly without policy pretraining achieved 45%, while Kimodo-Policy* with 419 hours of pretraining achieved an average success rate of 60%. This significantly outperformed GR00T N1.6 (31%) and $\Psi_{0}$ (35%). It achieved particularly high success rates on tasks requiring lower-body stability and whole-body coordination, such as punching a bag (90%) and sitting on a cushion (80%).

### 5.4 Motion Pretraining Selection and Scaling
With the same 282M-parameter Kimodo backbone, using RP-v1 pretrained on ~560 hours (67.63% success rate) yielded a 3.34-point gain in downstream performance over SEED-v1 pretrained on ~288 hours (64.29%). Furthermore, scaling pretraining data from 105 to 419 hours improved the success rate from 68.10% to 72.14%, and increasing trainable parameters also led to steady performance gains.

### 5.6 Ablations: Why is a Frozen Backbone Better?
Ablations across 3 Human-Object Interaction (HOI) tasks in HumanoidArena revealed striking results:
- **Random Initialization (w/o T2M)**: Success rate plummeted to just 18.33%.
- **Fine-Tuned Backbone (w/o Frozen)**: Rose only to 31.67%.
- **Frozen Pretrained Backbone (Proposed design)**: Jumped to 51.67% (and 56.11% with policy pretraining).

This confirms that preserving whole-body motion structures without disruption and adapting to vision purely via external adapters (ControlNet) is remarkably effective for robot control.

captions.F8: The 7 tasks in HumanoidArena used for evaluation. These include Human-Object Interaction (HOI) tasks such as soccer and box carrying, as well as Human-Scene Interaction (HSI) tasks like door opening, sofa sitting, and navigation, testing whole-body coordination and balance.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook: the frontier of kinematic foundation models for humanoids
sections.summary: This work validated the effectiveness of KAMs and Kimodo-Policy using a pretrained motion generation model as a backbone. The main limitation is its dependency on a specific whole-body tracker (SONIC); generalizing to diverse controllers and integrating with VLMs or video prediction models remain exciting directions.
sections.details:
This study introduced a new paradigm, KAMs, which adopts motion generation models directly as foundation backbones for humanoid action learning, and proved its viability with Kimodo-Policy. With only 92M trainable parameters, it leverages large-scale motion priors to achieve remarkable whole-body coordination in both simulation and the real world.

### Limitations
The primary limitation is its strong reliance on the low-level controller, the "SONIC tracker." Because the generated motion reference trajectories and deployment pipeline are tailored to SONIC, it remains unverified whether they can be directly applied to other trackers with different control dynamics or reference formats. Defining a more universal interface between high-level motion generation and low-level tracking is an important next step.

### Future Directions
A natural next step is combining KAM motion backbones with the advanced semantic reasoning of VLMs and the environmental prediction capabilities of video generation models. In addition, further enriching the expressiveness of the motion model itself—such as retargeting massive human motion capture datasets for robot pretraining—is expected to enable even more versatile and robust whole-body behaviors.

takeaways: Text-to-motion generation models can serve as effective pretraining backbones for humanoid action learning, alongside VLAs and WAMs.

Rather than fine-tuning the motion backbone downstream (31.67%), keeping it completely frozen and injecting vision via ControlNet (51.67%) preserves kinematic structure and yields vastly superior performance.
Combining inpainting conditioned on past motion history with short-chunk execution successfully transforms open-loop motion generators into smooth closed-loop controllers.
Because whole-body motion (root + body) and gripper states (hands) have fundamentally different characteristics, predicting them with separate heads decoupled by stop-gradients stabilizes training.
limitations: The interface design relies on a specific low-level whole-body tracker (SONIC), requiring validation and retuning to be ported to other controllers.
On certain Human-Object Interaction (HOI) tasks requiring millimeter-level precision at the hands or feet (e.g., soccer), it falls short of some specialized strong baselines.
Real-robot evaluations were limited to 10 trials per task; long-term reliability and robustness against unseen environmental disturbances remain to be fully validated.
